summaries.example: Imagine telling a friend, “Maya told Leo that she would win.” In speech, “she” might mean Maya or Leo. In a sign language, Maya and Leo can be placed in different spots in the signing space. Pointing to one spot can show who “she” means.
summaries.summary: Sign languages use hands, faces, body movements, and signing space to communicate meaning. The entry asks whether some visible parts of signing correspond to hidden parts of meaning in spoken language. A locus can mark a person or another kind of reference point. Pointing back to it can make a sentence clearer. Signers can also use space, repetition, movement, and body position to show time, amount, direction, events, or relationships. These visual patterns are called iconic when they resemble what they describe. The important puzzle is that sign language meaning seems to use both learned grammar and visual resemblance. Scholars are still studying whether these visible pieces are grammatical variables, features, iconic pictures, or combinations of these.
key_ideas: Sign languages are complete human languages, not merely collections of gestures.
Loci can help signers keep track of who or what a sentence is about.
Some sign languages may make hidden parts of meaning visible through space, movement, or body position.
Signs can combine ordinary, learned meanings with visual resemblance.
Researchers disagree about exactly what loci and role shift are in the grammar.
summaries.why_it_matters: This research shows that human language can work through sight as well as sound. It helps us understand sign languages on their own terms and improves general theories about meaning, reference, grammar, and communication. It also reminds us that a language can be systematic even when some of its forms are visually expressive.

important_terms.definition: The study of how language carries meaning, including how words, signs, grammar, and context work together.
A place in signing space that stands for a person, thing, time, possible situation, or sometimes a degree such as height.
A way of communicating in which part of a sign looks, moves, or is arranged like what it means.
A sign-language construction with a regular handshape but a position or movement that shows something about the thing being described.

questions_to_think_about: How could placing two people in different spots make a story easier to understand?
Can a movement show both what happened and how it happened?
Is a sign still language when part of its meaning comes from looking like something?
Why might different sign languages develop some similar features?

summaries.example: Suppose a signer first places “the students” in a broad area of signing space, then marks a smaller area for the students who came to class. Pointing to the remaining part can refer to the students who stayed home. The spatial arrangement contributes information that an ordinary English pronoun like “they” does not normally provide.
summaries.summary: The entry examines how sign languages illuminate foundational questions about meaning. Its central theme is Logical Visibility: components represented abstractly in theories of spoken-language meaning may receive overt expression in signing. Loci are the main case. A signer can associate discourse referents with positions in space and point back to them, sometimes for individuals, times, possible situations, or degrees. This supports a variable-like analysis, but loci also show feature-like behavior, so their precise grammatical status is unresolved. Other debated cases include movement patterns associated with telicity and Role Shift, which may involve context shift or instead a highly iconic, demonstrative construction. The entry then turns to iconicity. Signers can modify movement, repeat signs, arrange loci, and use classifier predicates so that form contributes visual information about events, quantities, or spatial relations. Formal pictorial semantics is one proposed tool for explaining these contributions. The broader conclusion is not that sign languages are identical, but that linguistic meaning may systematically integrate discrete grammar with iconic representation.
key_ideas: The Logical Visibility hypothesis holds that signing space can overtly realize elements such as variables, while the extent of this correspondence remains disputed.
Loci resemble variables because they can be created flexibly and track reference, but they can also behave like grammatical features; a mixed analysis is possible.
Temporal, modal, and degree-denoting loci have been used to argue that natural language may include variables for times, possible situations, and degrees.
Claims about visible telicity and role shift offer further cases of Logical Visibility, but iconic or demonstrative analyses provide alternatives.
Iconic modulation, repetition, classifier predicates, and role shift combine conventional grammar with visually interpreted form.
The cross-linguistic similarities of sign languages, and some findings about homesign and gesture, raise questions about modality, cognition, and language universals.
summaries.why_it_matters: Sign-language semantics challenges theories built mainly from spoken languages. It provides unusually direct evidence about reference, variables, tense, modality, degrees, event structure, quotation, and the boundary between grammar and gesture. It also encourages a more balanced comparison of sign and speech: speech should sometimes be studied together with gesture, while sign should not be reduced to gesture. The open debates matter because they concern what kinds of entities and structures a general theory of human language must recognize.

important_terms.definition: The study of how linguistic expressions contribute to meaning and how those meanings combine with context and grammar.
A position or region in signing space associated with a discourse referent; loci can be linked to individuals, times, possible situations, or degrees.
The proposal that a sign language can overtly express a logical or grammatical element that is usually unpronounced in spoken language.
A meaning relation in which an expression partly denotes something because its form preserves relevant structural or perceptual properties of that thing.
A property of a predicate describing whether its event has a natural endpoint, as in arrive, rather than an open-ended activity such as wait.
A proposed operation that changes the context from which indexicals such as “I,” “you,” or “now” are interpreted; in signing it has been linked to body rotation.
A lexical sign for a class of entities whose handshape is conventional but whose position, orientation, or movement is interpreted iconically.
A theory in which pictures or picture-like forms are evaluated by asking what objects or situations could project onto them from a viewpoint.

questions_to_think_about: What evidence would distinguish a locus that is a logical variable from one that is merely a grammatical feature?
If a sign’s movement shows an endpoint, does that prove that telicity is morphologically encoded?
Why might classifier predicates and gestures favor an order that follows what an observer would see?
Can iconic meaning be part of the truth conditions of a sentence, rather than an extra suggestion?
Which similarities among sign languages might come from grammar, iconicity, or properties of visual communication?

summaries.example: A signer might introduce a soccer player on the left and a coach on the right. Later, pointing left can mean “the player,” while pointing right can mean “the coach.” The signer can also show “the player ran” with a movement that has a clear stopping point, or repeat a sign to suggest several players or events.
summaries.summary: Sign Language Semantics explores what sign languages teach us about meaning and grammar. A major question is whether signing space makes normally hidden logical structure visible. Loci can be assigned to people or other discourse referents, and later pointing can identify them. This resembles the work of variables in semantic theories, though loci may also behave like grammatical features. Similar proposals concern loci for times, possible situations, and degrees. Researchers also study whether sharp movement endings mark telicity and whether Role Shift openly marks a change in context. The entry emphasizes that iconicity is not just decoration. Movement, repetition, orientation, and spatial arrangement can contribute meaning, sometimes as part of the main claim of a sentence. Classifier predicates especially combine conventional categories with picture-like information. Comparisons with speech and gesture suggest that sign languages may make visual meaning more deeply grammatical, although the exact analysis remains unsettled.
key_ideas: Sign languages have rich grammars and should be included in general theories of human language.
Loci can make reference clearer by linking pronouns or agreement verbs to locations in space.
Some researchers treat loci as visible variables; others compare them to grammatical features, and hybrid proposals combine both ideas.
Movement and body position may express abstract grammatical meanings, but iconicity offers competing explanations.
Repetition can mark plural objects or events while also showing number, arrangement, or speed.
Classifier predicates have learned, conventional parts and iconic parts that depict position or movement.
summaries.why_it_matters: The topic matters because it broadens our picture of language. Sign languages show that grammar can use three-dimensional space, movement, facial expression, and visual resemblance while remaining systematic. Their patterns help philosophers and linguists ask what a variable is, how reference works, how events are structured, and how much meaning can come from an iconic form. The research also highlights genuine variation and ongoing disagreement rather than treating one analysis as settled.

important_terms.definition: The part of linguistics that studies how expressions, sentences, and context produce meaning.
A spot or area in signing space connected with a person, object, time, or other thing being discussed.
The idea that a sign language may show a grammatical or logical element openly when spoken languages often leave it unspoken.
A connection between a form and its meaning based partly on resemblance, such as a movement that pictures a path or speed.
Whether an event description includes a built-in natural finish, as arrive does, unlike an activity such as wait.
A way of changing whose point of view supplies the meaning of words such as “I” or “you,” sometimes marked by turning the body.
A sign with a conventional handshape for a type of thing whose direction, position, or movement gives extra visual information.
A meaning system for picture-like forms that explains what objects or situations a visual representation can describe.

questions_to_think_about: When does pointing count as grammar rather than an ordinary gesture?
Could a location stand for a time or a possible situation as well as a person?
What would be a good test for deciding whether a sign’s stopping movement marks telicity?
Why might a repeated sign mean “exactly three” in one form but “at least several” in another?
Should sign languages and spoken languages be compared without including gesture?
